standard_prerequisites.name: n-connected maps and the fixed-level induction principle
standard_prerequisites.statement: A map f : A -> B is n-connected when all its fibres are n-connected; the book's Lemma 7.5.7 states that for fixed n, precomposition (blank o f) is an equivalence for every family P : B -> n-Type.
standard_prerequisites.use: That lemma is the base case k = n of the retained induction (source line 1576) and is cited again for the family Q at source lines 1585-1588.

standard_prerequisites.name: Fibres, sigma types and paths between dependent pairs
standard_prerequisites.statement: The fibre of a map g at a point is Sm{x}(g(x) = point); elements of a sigma type are equal as soon as their components are, with the second component compared after transport.
standard_prerequisites.use: The proof computes the fibre of the precomposition map at source line 1580 and the identity type of two of its elements at source lines 1581-1584.

standard_prerequisites.name: Truncatedness of path spaces and of function types into truncated families
standard_prerequisites.statement: If P is a family of (k+1)-types then b |-> (g(b) = h(b)) is a family of k-types; and a type is m-truncated as soon as all its path spaces are (m-1)-truncated.
standard_prerequisites.use: These two facts close the induction step at source lines 1588-1589.

core_obligations: Induct on the natural number k - n, using the fixed-level induction principle as the base case k = n (source lines 1575-1576).
In the inductive step, compute the fibre of (blank o f) at l : Prd{a:A} P(f(a)) as Sm{g : Prd{b:B} P(b)} Prd{a:A} g(f(a)) = l(a) (source lines 1579-1580).

Compute the identity type of two elements (g,p) and (h,q) of that fibre as Sm{r : g ~ h} (r o f = p . q^-1), reducing the comparison of dependent pairs to a homotopy together with a coherence path (source lines 1581-1584).
Recognise that right-hand type as the fibre of the same precomposition map for the family Q(b) := (g(b) = h(b)), so that the inductive hypothesis applies to it (source lines 1585-1588).
Conclude that all path spaces of the fibre of (blank o f) at l are (k-n-2)-types, hence that the fibre is (k-n-1)-truncated, which is the claim (source lines 1588-1589).

proof_roadmap.step: Induct on k - n with the fixed-level induction principle as base case.
Compute the fibre of the precomposition map at a section l.
Compute the identity type of two points of that fibre.
Identify that type as the fibre for the family of path types and apply the inductive hypothesis.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is Lemma 8.6.1 at source lines 1569-1572: for an n-connected f and a family P of k-types with k >= n, the precomposition map (blank o f) is (k-n-2)-truncated, proved at source lines 1574-1590. The proof inducts on k - n with the fixed-level induction principle as base case (source line 1576) and then has to make the level drop by exactly one. That requires computing the fibre of (blank o f) at a section l as Sm{g : Prd{b:B}P(b)} Prd{a:A} g(f(a)) = l(a) (line 1580), computing the identity type of two such pairs as Sm{r : g ~ h} (r o f = p . q^-1) (lines 1582-1584), and then recognising that last type as the fibre of the same precomposition map for the family Q(b) := (g(b) = h(b)) (lines 1585-1587). Only because P is a family of (k+1)-types is Q a family of k-types, so the inductive hypothesis applies and yields that all path spaces of the original fibre are (k-n-2)-types (lines 1588-1589). The variable level is what makes this non-routine: the statement shifts the truncation index at each induction step, and the fibre and identity-type computations have to be set up so that their own level drops accordingly.
